newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Far East may eye U.S. grain imports - trade.
newsitem.headline: Russian Far East may eye U.S. grain imports - trade.

text.p: Russia's Far East may be trying to pull together financing for U.S. wheat imports, trade sources said on Friday.
"There are steps in the direction of imports," one source said. "But it's a tricky question and a matter of financing."

A second source, commenting on remarks by Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun in August that Russia may buy 500,000 tonnes of food wheat from North America or Australia, said, "I would think they'll be in the market for slightly more."
Another source said late last month that he thought the Far East could seek a half million tonnes of U.S. hard red winter wheat for November or December delivery.
"The need (in the Far East) is there," a fourth source said.

Eastern Siberia, the region from which it would be cheapest to send grain eastward to the Russian Far East, is likely to have a net wheat harvest of 1.9 million tonnes, below 1995's average 2.4 million tonnes.
Demand in the Far East -- a huge, sparsely-populated area ranging from Vladivostok in the south to frozen Chukotka by the Bering Sea -- needs only about 300,000 tonnes of food wheat a year.

But Vladivostok is an ideal entry point for grain imports intended for other needy regions. Supplies can be shipped from Vladivostok by rail to Siberian or Far North regions more cheaply than can wheat from Russia's grain belt.
"I know that Yakutia (the diamond-producing region, in northeastern Siberia) is running around trying to find wheat," one of the sources said.
Russia is facing its second poor grain harvest in a row, with official net forecasts ranging from 72 to 78 million tonnes and independent forecasts around the 69 million tonne mark.
Khlystun had also said imports of 4.0-4.5 million tonnnes of feed grains, mostly maize and soymeal, were possible.
Russia's net 1996 wheat crop is seen at about 34 million tonnes.

Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd said that less than one-third of the crop was third-class milling wheat (a Russian standard), less than one-third was fourth class (a grade that requires blending with higher quality material), and the rest was usable only as feed grain.
Russia's annual food wheat demand is 17-18 million tonnes.
